overview.text: Teeth are hard structures anchored in the jaws that help animals grasp, cut, tear, crush, or grind food. Their shapes often reflect their jobs: in mammals, incisors cut, pointed canines can seize or tear, and broader premolars and molars crush and grind. A human tooth has a crown above the gum and a root set in the jaw; enamel covers the crown, dentin forms the hard layer beneath it, and a pulp chamber contains nerves and blood vessels. Teeth matter not only for feeding: because mammals have different tooth shapes, scientists can use teeth in skulls as clues to diet and way of life.

key_facts.text: A human tooth has a crown and a root; enamel covers the crown, while dentin surrounds the pulp, which contains nerves and blood vessels.
Human incisors are shaped for cutting, canines for tearing, and premolars and molars for crushing and grinding food.
Among mammals, tooth shapes vary with diet: for example, many plant-eaters have broad, flat molars for grinding vegetation, while carnivores often have sharp canines for catching and tearing prey.
Scientists can study a mammal’s teeth and skull to infer aspects of how it lived, including whether it ate meat, plants, or both.
The tissues that support teeth include the gums, periodontal ligament, and jawbone; the tooth root is covered by cementum.
